_comment: Academic prompt bank for adapt-grow-promptbuilder. TWO parts: `formulas` (named prompt frameworks, each listing its ordered steps + an assembly template) and `banks` (reusable phrase libraries the steps draw on). A lesson picks a formula; each step's `bank` names the phrase library that fills its dropdown. The component is label-driven, so the same engine drives an academic prompt builder OR a phrase generator just by changing the data. Sheffield's Academic GenAI Prompt Bank categories are mapped pedagogically as the sub-categories (optgroup labels) in the `task` bank; prompts are reworded and extended. Fill-ins are in [square brackets]. No em-dashes (house rule). Attribution: University of Sheffield Academic Skills, Academic GenAI Prompt Bank.

costar.name: CO-STAR
costar.subtitle: Context, Objective, Style, Tone, Audience, Response
costar.bestFor: Polished writing where voice and audience matter.
costar.template: {context} {objective} Write in a {style} style and a {tone} tone for {audience}. {response}

risen.name: RISEN
risen.subtitle: Role, Instruction, Steps, End goal, Narrowing
risen.bestFor: Bigger tasks that need structure and constraints.

role.label: Expertise
items: an expert in [subject]
an academic tutor on my [subject] course
a researcher who knows the literature on [topic]

role.label: Academic practice support
items: an academic practice specialist who helps me develop how I study and write
an academic practice specialist in [academic practice, e.g. criticality]
an academic librarian who helps me find and evaluate sources
an academic librarian who helps me reference accurately

role.label: Support style
items: a study-skills tutor who explains things simply
a critical friend who challenges my reasoning
an examiner marking against the grade criteria
an English-language tutor (English is my second language)

role.label: Audience voice
items: writing for an academic audience
explaining to a non-specialist audience

task.label: Background research
items: Trace how [concept] developed and why it matters today.
Compare and contrast [two theories] in [subject], with strengths and weaknesses.
Explore the impact of [innovation] on [field], short and long term.
Examine where [subject] and [another subject] intersect.
Outline the main debates in [topic] and what is at stake.

task.label: Be critical
items: Give a range of critical perspectives on this claim: [claim].
Set out the weaknesses or limits of [theory] and the alternatives.
Give the strongest counter-arguments to [idea].
What controversies surround [topic], and why do they matter?
Whose perspectives are missing from this, and why?

task.label: Understand a concept
items: Explain [concept] in plain language for someone new to it.
Summarise [theory] as five key points I must know, and why.
Use an everyday analogy to explain [concept].
Give a step-by-step breakdown of [concept] for a beginner.
List common misconceptions about [concept] and correct them.

task.label: Feedback: structure
items: Is the structure of this logical and coherent? [paste your draft]
How strong and clear are my introduction and thesis? [paste your draft]
Is my main argument supported all the way through? [paste your draft]
How effective is my conclusion at pulling the argument together? [paste your draft]

task.label: Feedback: language
items: Is my language clear and easy to follow? [paste your draft]
Comment on my academic style and tone, and suggest improvements. [paste your draft]
Check for grammar, punctuation and syntax issues. [paste your draft]

task.label: Feedback: use of sources
items: How well do I synthesise the literature here? [paste your draft]
Are my claims properly supported by evidence? [paste your draft]
Identify gaps or limits in my use of sources. [paste your draft]

task.label: Exam revision
items: Ask me short-answer questions on [topic] one at a time, with feedback after each.
Make flashcards to test me on [topic].
Break [topic] into short, memorable key points.
What should I focus on revising for a [level] exam in [topic]?
Build a spaced-repetition revision timetable for my exam on [date]: [topics].

task.label: Productivity
items: Evaluate the tone of this email. [paste email]
List the actions arising from this email. [paste email]
Redraft this in a more formal tone. [paste text]
Plan intermediate deadlines for an essay due in [time].
Give me five concepts to prepare before a lecture on [topic].

task.label: Follow-on (after a reply)
items: Expand on point [number] in more detail.
Give case studies to illustrate these points.
Give counter-arguments to each of these points.
Where can I find more data on [topic]?
Which views are under-represented here, and why?

context.label: Your level
items: I am a first-year (Level 4) undergraduate.
I am a second-year (Level 5) undergraduate.
I am a final-year (Level 6) undergraduate.
I am a Master's (Level 7) student.
I am a PhD researcher.

context.label: About you
items: I am studying [module or topic].
My strengths are [x] and [x].
My challenges are [x] and [x].
English is my second language.
My work is influenced by the ideas of [x].

format.label: Length
items: Keep it under 500 words.
Use no more than five paragraphs.

format.label: Form
items: Give a numbered list.
Write in prose, not bullet points.
Present it as questions and answers.

format.label: Study integrity
items: Explain it, do not write it for me.
Avoid the first person.
Show your reasoning so I can check it.

audience.label: Audience
items: a non-specialist reader
fellow students on my course
an academic marker
someone completely new to the topic

tone.label: Tone
items: formal
objective and neutral
encouraging
direct and concise

style.label: Style
items: academic
plain English
structured and signposted
critical and analytical

steps.label: Approach
items: Work through it step by step.
Break it into numbered stages.
Show your reasoning as you go.
Ask me one question at a time and wait for my answer.

goal.label: End goal
items: so that I can revise it independently.
so that I understand the method, not just the answer.
so that I can improve my next draft.
so that I am ready for the assessment.

benchmark.label: Knowledge
items: so that I get better at building secure knowledge of my subject’s core content.
so that I get better at understanding the key theories, concepts and debates.
so that I get better at knowing how my field developed and where it stands now.

benchmark.label: Thinking
items: so that I get better at breaking problems down and solving them with my subject’s methods.
so that I get better at weighing evidence and arguments to reach a reasoned judgement.

benchmark.label: Application
items: so that I get better at applying what I know to real problems.
so that I get better at using the right research and enquiry methods.
so that I get better at finding and using information and sources well.
so that I get better at working with data, numbers and quantitative reasoning.
so that I get better at building my digital skills.
so that I get better at being more enterprising and creative.

benchmark.label: Communication
items: so that I get better at communicating clearly to different audiences.
so that I get better at working well as part of a team.
so that I get better at writing clearly in the forms my subject needs.

benchmark.label: Autonomy & integrity
items: so that I get better at working ethically and with integrity.
so that I get better at becoming a more independent, self-directed learner.
so that I get better at understanding sustainability in my field.
so that I get better at developing professional practice and employability.
so that I get better at reflecting on my learning and developing.
so that I get better at understanding equality, diversity and inclusion in my field.

benchmarks._comment: Universal graduate benchmarks (the shared core distilled from the 54 QAA subject benchmark statements), cross-referenced into this prompt bank so a student can think about which graduate skill / graduate attribute (academic practice) they are building. House term: use "graduate skill", "graduate attribute", "graduate competency" or "academic practice" - NOT "academic skills". `think` = the student-facing focus; the `benchmark` bank surfaces these as a pickable category; each task category lists the benchmark ids it most develops. Source of record: catalogue/context/subject/benchmarks/universal-reference.json.
